analysis.one_liner: Bans commercial logging on federal public lands, replacing it with restoration work and retraining for timber workers.
analysis.headline: A bill to end commercial logging on federal lands drew 100 House cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have outlawed commercial logging and timber sales on National Forests, National Parks, Wildlife Refuges, and Bureau of Land Management lands, with a two-year phase-out for existing contracts. It proposed to redirect the money the government spends subsidizing logging into a restoration corps that would repair logged lands, plus retraining grants for laid-off timber workers. It was referred to three committees and their subcommittees and never went any further.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who the bill says lose money on every federal timber sale because the Forest Service spends more preparing and administering sales than it collects in return. People who use national forests for recreation, fishing, and hunting, since the bill argues logging destroys habitat and watersheds. Dislocated timber workers would get retraining grants, job search and relocation allowances, needs-related income support, and hiring preference in the new restoration corps. Rural counties would keep receiving timber receipt payments through fiscal year 2003.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits all commercial logging and timber sales on National Forest, National Park, National Wildlife Refuge, and BLM lands, with a two-year phase-out for existing contracts and immediate suspension of sales in roadless areas.

Cites GAO reports finding that only a small fraction of the hundreds of millions of dollars annually spent on the Forest Service timber sales program returns to the Treasury, framing the program as a net loss to taxpayers.

Creates a Natural Heritage Restoration Corps to reforest logged areas, decommission logging roads, and stabilize slopes, with hiring preference for timber workers who lose their jobs because of the act.

Authorizes worker retraining grants of up to $100 million in the first year and $150 million in later years, including job search and relocation allowances and income support tied to training participation.
Keeps revenue-sharing payments to timber counties flowing at roughly $125 million per year through fiscal 2003, guaranteeing those communities their payments regardless of logging levels.

Notes that Forest Service polls show most Americans oppose producing consumer goods from federal lands, that federal timber supplies under five percent of US timber consumption, and that recreation on national forests generates over 30 times more jobs and income than logging.

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies would lose their subsidized supply of federal timber and could file claims for terminated contracts, paid from logging accounts. Logging and mill workers in rural timber towns would lose jobs, partially offset by the retraining program. Paper and wood-products manufacturers would face a modestly smaller wood supply, though federal lands provide under five percent of US timber consumption.
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber companies and rural logging towns

drawbacks.text: Ending federal logging would eliminate jobs in rural communities that depend on timber payrolls and county timber payments; the retraining grants and hiring preference in the restoration corps soften but do not erase that loss.

The federal government would have to pay damages or negotiated settlements for every existing timber contract it terminates during the phase-out, including payments to purchasers whose contracts are suspended immediately in roadless areas.

The prohibition is broad — it covers standing, fallen, living, and dead timber and allows only personal-use firewood gathering — so supporters of mechanical thinning to reduce wildfire risk would lose that tool on federal lands, even as the bill's own findings cite a congressionally commissioned study concluding logging increased fire risk and severity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For taxpayers and forest users, the arithmetic is favorable: the bill's own findings document that the federal logging program loses money, while recreation generates far more economic activity than timber sales, and federal timber is a small slice of national supply. The real costs fall on a geographically concentrated group — timber workers and rural counties — and the bill tries to address them with retraining and guaranteed county payments through 2003, but a two-year phase-out would still be disruptive for communities built around mills. The design is more thorough than most phase-out bills, though claims for terminated contracts add short-term cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees and bounced among five subcommittees, but no committee ever held it a hearing or markup, and it never came to a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Representative Cynthia McKinney introduced the bill on April 13, 1999 with 48 original cosponsors, framing it as ending corporate welfare and saving taxpayers money.
The bill reached 100 cosponsors — 96 Democrats and 4 Republicans.
The same day it was introduced, the House referred it to the Agriculture, Resources, and Education and the Workforce Committees.

Within a week it was referred to subcommittees including Forests and Forest Health, National Parks and Public Lands, and Fisheries Conservation, Wildlife and Oceans, and executive comment was requested from the Departments of Agriculture and Interior.
No further action of any kind was taken; the bill died in committee when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber companies kept buying federally subsidized timber for two more years at below-cost prices, and taxpayers kept covering the difference. No land, worker, or budget outcome changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber companies that kept subsidized access

for.name: Cynthia McKinney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 47 original cosponsors.

for.name: Jim Leach
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, one of the few Republicans on the bill.

against.name: House Agriculture, Resources, and Education and Workforce Committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it sat in committee and subcommittees for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Timber industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on federal logging, which the bill would have ended entirely.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 96 of 100 — with only 4 Republican supporters out of 223 House Republicans, and the Republican-run committees of jurisdiction never moved the bill; no floor vote ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill ends their access to federal timber sold below the cost of preparing and administering the sales, which GAO reports cited in the bill show costs taxpayers hundreds of millions a year. Their supply would shrink, and they could claim damages for terminated contracts.

industries.industry: Recreation and tourism on national forests
industries.note: The bill cites Forest Service figures that recreation and tourism generate over 30 times more jobs and income on national forests than logging, and ends activities it says damage watersheds, fisheries, and scenery those businesses depend on.

The bill directs up to $33 million from logging accounts to the EPA to study and fund development of wood-free paper and building products, creating a research and grant pipeline for competitors to wood products.
